To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the surface quality of laser milled components depends on the pulse duration.

(i) the surface integrity of laser milled microcomponents is directly related to the heat transfer into the bulk; (ii) ultra-short laser pulses are more efficient in terms of material removal and surface roughness; (iii) the surface roughness of laser milled features is mainly affected by the laser pulse duration and not the laser fluence; (iv) the material removal mechanism is different in micro- and nanoseconds and in ultra-short pulses; (v) the heat-affected zones
the surface quality and the heat-affected zones on the processed surface are strongly affected by laser pulse duration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the surface quality and microstructural changes of a material commonly used in microtooling applications.
the effects of pulse durations on the surface quality and the resulting microstructure.
the surface integrity and material microstructure after laser milling of engineering materials using different pulse durations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the surface integrity is not as affected when working in the ultra-short pulse regimes, but the removal rate is significantly lower.
the surface roughness and the heat-affected zones are directly linked with the pulse energy, while the microstructure and material removal rate are linked with the pulse duration.
the surface integrity of the laser milled microstructures is strongly dependent on pulse duration and that the surface quality is better for shorter pulses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
laser milling of engineering materials using micro- to nanosecond pulses is more likely to induce surface defects and structural changes in the material than ultra-short pulsed ablation.

the use of ultra-short pulsed lasers for laser milling of engineering materials would lead to a reduction in heat-affected zone, and hence to improved surface quality and microstructure of the machined surface.
the surface integrity of a laser milled surface is directly affected by the pulse duration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of longer pulse durations (micro- and nanoseconds) is not recommended when processing high-strength materials such as tool steel.

when ablating with ultra-short pulsed lasers it is possible to achieve surface roughness in the order of 0.1 μm, which is a 10-fold improvement compared to the results obtained with micro- and nanoseconds pulses.
laser processing in pico- or femtosecond regime is a viable alternative for producing high-precision microcomponents with high surface quality.
